newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Frost hits west as Poland reports crop loss.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Frost hits west as Poland reports crop loss.

text.p: Western Europe, where farmers are more used to worrying about drought than cold, has seen snow in places and widespread frost in the last 24 hours.
News Poland has lost a chunk of its grain and oilseed crops to the cold weather has driven home how weather sensitive agriculture can be.

The winter has ruined about 12 percent of Poland's grain and rapeseed crop, with about 600,000 hectares in the process of being ploughed under, the Central Statistical Office (GUS) said in a statement on Wednesday.
Unsettled weather continued across most of the French grain and sugar belts on Wednesday, but showers were becoming more scattered and accompanied by strong winds, weather office Meteo France said.
Moderate showers fell across parts of the southwest, where steady rain earlier this week allowed farmers to resume maize sowings delayed by weeks of drought.
Light snow fell at the southern tip of the Paris grain basin near Tours.
Meteo France said showers were darting quickly eastwards, with storms in many areas and gusts up to 80 km per hour in the northwest.
Maximum temperatures were below normal for the time of year at 6-10 degrees Celsius in northern France and 10-16 degrees in the south.

Frost was widespread in the southern part of the UK overnight on Tuesday into Wednesday, with only limited rain falling on the important eastern agricultural areas, according to the London Weather Centre.
Forecasters expected more frost in the early hours of Thursday, but farmers reckoned it would have little or no adverse impact on crops.
"Yorkshire into Lincolnshire, East Anglia and the Midlands had widespread frost last night," a spokeswoman said.
The lowest temperature was minus four degrees Celsius at one place in Oxfordshire, while temperatures of around minus two were recorded in East Anglia.

"It hasn't caused us any serious concern," one big East Anglian farmer said. "We had one (frost) at minus four a couple of weeks ago and I was a bit worried about that, but there was no lasting impact," he said.

Rain over the last 24 hours has been too little to have any great impact on crops in moisture-sensitive East Anglia. The highest rainfall in the day to 1000 GMT this morning was at one reporting station in Norfolk, which got 1.8 millimeters. But most areas got less than one millimeter, the London Weather Centre said.
According to the Meteorological Office, a longer spell of rain will cross most parts late Wednesday, with frost in the east towards dawn.
Freak winds of up to 100 kilometres per hour and scattered hail hit the north of Spain on Tuesday, damaging cereal crops in the Catalan province of Lleida, the civil protection agency said.
Gusts of up to 75 km per hour are forecast to hit the barley-growing region of Castille-La Mancha on Wednesday, the national weather service said.
The area produced much of Spain's barley crop last year, according to official data.
Farmers' associations estimated that about 60 percent of the winter cereal crop in Lleida had been damaged by hailstorms which started late Monday. Peach and pear orchards also suffered damage.
Lleida produced about 650,000 tonnes of cereals in 1996, primarily soft wheat.
In the northwestern region of Galicia, rough seas forced fishing fleets to stay in port.

An abnormal combination of drought and frost affecting large areas of Italy for the past three months has hit fruit crops, but it is too soon to assess damage to cereals, an official of the Italian agricultural producers' association Confagricoltura said.
"Cold and lack of rain can certainly cause problems for cereals and the yields could be down, but we won't see the effects until July," he said.
Durum and soft wheat sowings in Italy have already taken place while maize sowings are just starting.

According to independent forecaster Weather Services Corporation, drought-breaking rains in the west of Europe will continue for a few more days in areas such as northern Spain, France, Benelux and the UK.
Higher than normal temperatures dominate eastern Europe and western areas of the former Soviet Union, but with some showers too.
Showers and lower temperatures are pushing eastward in central parts of the former Soviet Union.
